title: Inequality is crossing wealth, climate responsibility, unpaid care, global finance, and political representation rather than remaining a single income gap
source_unit: World Inequality Lab, World Inequality Report 2026
geography: Global income, wealth, gender, climate, financial, regional, taxation, and political inequality across countries and regions

denominator.unit: global population income and wealth distribution frame

top_income_share.value: the global top 10 percent earn more than the remaining 90 percent combined

bottom_income_share.value: the poorest half captures less than 10 percent of global income

top_wealth_share.unit: percent of global wealth owned by the top 10 percent

bottom_wealth_share.unit: percent of global wealth held by the bottom half

wealth_concentration.value: wealth concentration has increased as billionaire and centi-millionaire wealth grew faster than the bottom half's wealth

observations.method: World Inequality Database analysis and synthesis drawing on work from more than 200 scholars and distributional estimates across income and wealth.
observations.uncertainty: Global distribution estimates combine tax, national-account, survey, and modeling sources with uneven coverage; thresholds, imputation, and purchasing-power adjustments affect comparisons and do not reveal every household's lived condition.
observations.subgroup: The global top and bottom income and wealth groups, middle classes, countries with different data coverage, households with different assets and debts, and policymakers considering redistribution.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aggregate concentration can coexist with broad absolute gains in living standards; wealth measures differ from disposable income, consumption, security, and political influence in particular settings.

denominator.unit: global emissions associated with private capital ownership

top_ten_capital_emissions.unit: percent of emissions associated with private capital ownership attributed to the global top 10 percent

top_one_capital_emissions.unit: percent of emissions associated with private capital ownership attributed to the global top 1 percent

bottom_half_capital_emissions.unit: percent of emissions associated with private capital ownership attributed to the global bottom half

responsibility_exposure.value: those contributing least to capital-ownership emissions are often more exposed to climate shocks and have fewer adaptation resources

observations.method: WIR synthesis of research allocating emissions associated with privately owned capital to wealth holders, alongside global distributional and climate-exposure analysis.
observations.uncertainty: Capital-ownership emissions differ from direct household consumption emissions and exclude emissions from publicly owned assets; attribution, asset ownership, and exposure measures involve methodological assumptions.
observations.subgroup: Wealth groups, capital owners, workers and households exposed to climate hazards, low-income countries, investors, public authorities, and communities with unequal adaptation capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Capital-based attribution can complement rather than replace consumption-based accounting; high emitters may face policy constraints while low-emitting populations can still have important local environmental impacts.

denominator.unit: global paid and unpaid labor comparison frame

women_labor_income_share.value: women capture just over one-quarter of total global labor income

weekly_work_hours.value: women work about 53 hours per week versus 43 for men when paid, domestic, and care work are combined

hourly_income_paid_only.unit: percent of men's hourly income earned by women when unpaid work is excluded

hourly_income_including_unpaid.unit: percent of men's hourly income earned by women when unpaid domestic labor is included

care_conversion.value: unpaid domestic and care labor changes the measured distribution of work, income, opportunity, and political participation

observations.method: WIR gender analysis combining labor-income distributions with time-use and unpaid domestic and care-work accounting.
observations.uncertainty: Cross-country time-use, income, and valuation methods differ; hourly-income comparisons are constructed measures and do not capture bargaining, job quality, wealth, or within-household allocation fully.
observations.subgroup: Women and men, unpaid caregivers, parents, households with different care demands, workers in paid and unpaid activities, and policymakers designing care and labor reforms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Unpaid work can provide care, autonomy, and household value not fully represented by income metrics; paid and unpaid work may be complementary rather than interchangeable.

observations.period: 2025-2026; global finance, human capital, and political cleavages

denominator.unit: global inequality, finance, opportunity, and political-coalition framework

net_foreign_income_transfer.unit: percent of global GDP transferred annually from poorer to richer nations through net foreign-income flows, approximately

education_spending_gap.value: average education spending per child is approximately 40 times higher in Europe and North America/Oceania than in Sub-Saharan Africa

redistribution_effect.value: tax-and-transfer systems reduce income gaps by more than 30 percent in Europe and North America/Oceania, according to the report's regional comparison

territorial_political_divide.value: political-affiliation gaps between metropolitan centers and smaller towns have reached historically high levels in many advanced democracies

coalition_route.value: unequal services, job opportunity, trade-shock exposure, and campaign-finance concentration can weaken coalitions for redistribution

observations.method: WIR comparative synthesis of global financial flows, regional education spending, tax-and-transfer systems, territorial inequality, political affiliation, and campaign-finance evidence.
observations.uncertainty: These are aggregate cross-country and regional relationships; the report does not establish a single causal pathway from finance or geography to individual political behavior, and estimates vary with definitions and coverage.
observations.subgroup: Borrowing and lending countries, students and families, metropolitan and smaller-town residents, workers exposed to trade shocks, political parties, donors, and redistributive institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Global financial flows can also reflect risk, investment returns, or productive capital allocation; territorial political divides may arise from culture, identity, or institutions in addition to material inequality.

related_sources.claim: World Inequality Database provides the underlying distributional data platform and methodology context.
Official WIR 2026 methodology and data-construction context.

boundary: This record adds a cross-domain inequality route across income, wealth, capital-linked climate responsibility, unpaid care, human-capital access, global finance, taxation, territorial divides, and democratic coalitions. It uses World Inequality Lab aggregate distributional estimates and synthesis, not respondent-level income or political histories, household budgets, firm ownership files, individual emissions footprints, causal climate effects, or proof that any single policy produces equal outcomes everywhere.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Inequality Report 2026 executive summary reviewed for global income and wealth concentration, capital-ownership emissions, gendered paid and unpaid work, global financial transfers, regional education spending, redistribution, and territorial political cleavages.
